Plotting species introductions between continents

Source: vignettes/plotting_introductions.Rmd
plotting_introductions.Rmd

Here in this article, we show how to use the package’s function introGraph to plot where the species of any plant family or genus were introduced from and to. The graphic is a heatmap with the number of species native to each continent (rows) that are introduced in each other continent (columns), following the World Geographical Scheme for Recording Plant Distributions. It helps to see which floras are the main sources of introduced plants, and which continents receive most of them.


Setup

Install the latest development version of expowo from GitHub:

#install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("DBOSlab/expowo")
library(expowo)


1. Mining the species list and their distribution

introGraph uses as input data the species list and their native and introduced distribution returned by powoSpecies. The first search downloads the data of the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (about 90 MB) only once, so any following search takes a few seconds.

fab <- powoSpecies(family = "Fabaceae",
                   verbose = FALSE)


2. Plotting introductions between continents

Just provide the output of powoSpecies to introGraph. Each botanical country of the native and introduced distribution of each species is assigned to its continent, and a species counts once for each pair of continents. Introductions within the same continent are not shown. No download is needed, as the continent of each botanical country is stored within expowo. Setting save = TRUE writes the graphic within a subfolder named after the current date, in any of the formats JPG, PDF, PNG or TIFF.

introGraph(inputdf = fab,
           save = TRUE,
           dir = "results_introGraph",
           filename = "intro_graph_Fabaceae",
           format = "png")

FIGURE 1. Number of Fabaceae species native to each continent (rows) that are introduced in each other continent (columns).


About 1,300 legume species are introduced in another continent. Species native to temperate Asia, i.e. the Mediterranean and western Asian clovers, medicks and vetches, are the most widely introduced, above all in Europe, Africa and Northern America. Africa and tropical Asia are also major sources of introduced legumes. The Antarctic continent of the scheme includes the subantarctic islands, where some legumes were introduced.


3. Plotting introductions between regions

For a finer view, the argument level = "region" uses the 52 regions of the level 2 of the scheme (e.g. Brazil, Southwestern Europe, Indo-China) instead of the nine continents. The graphic is larger, and it is saved with a larger size accordingly.

introGraph(inputdf = fab,
           level = "region",
           save = TRUE,
           dir = "results_introGraph",
           filename = "intro_graph_Fabaceae_regions",
           format = "pdf")


4. Using the graphic object

introGraph returns a ggplot object, so the graphic can be customised with any function of ggplot2. The data of the graphic has the number of species (species) native to each continent or region (from) that are introduced in another one (to).

p <- introGraph(fab, verbose = FALSE)

# Main routes of introduction
routes <- p$data[order(-p$data$species), c("from", "to", "species")]
head(routes)

# Adding a title
p + ggplot2::ggtitle("Where legumes were introduced")


When the input data has synonyms (a status column, as in powoSpecies(synonyms = TRUE)), only accepted species are counted.


5. Reference

Govaerts, R., E. Nic Lughadha, N. Black, R. Turner, and A. Paton. 2021. The World Checklist of Vascular Plants, a continuously updated resource for exploring global plant diversity. Scientific Data 8: 215.
